A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same REFORM research work and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–G. The additions can be distinguished reliably from retained and relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original failure-discovery, reward-robustness, and downstream alignment experiments on Anthropic HH and PKU Beavertails, including additional analyses and examples in the appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds GPT-4 judging, Qwen 2.5 14B robustness results, and comparisons with RRM.

M1.justification: The controlled-decoding procedure, reward objectives, selection of the lowest-loss 5% of training examples, and failure-aware augmentation remain unchanged. Appendix G retains the implementation; evaluating Qwen does not introduce a documented method adaptation.

E1.justification: Both versions use Anthropic HH and PKU Beavertails for the same preference-modeling and alignment tasks, including the same four perturbation categories. The additional backbone and judge change experimental configurations, not dataset or task coverage.

E2.justification: Figure 6 adds RRM as an evaluated competing reward-training method. This substantially expands the robustness comparison beyond v1's original-reward control to an alternative robustness method. Random perturbation and attribute-based prompting remain the failure-discovery comparators.

E3.justification: The existing evaluation design is extended with GPT-4 alongside Gemini for appropriateness judging and Qwen 2.5 14B alongside Mistral 7B for robustness testing. The stated test sampling, metrics, perturbation procedures, and BoN/PPO/DPO settings are retained.

E4.justification: Figure 5 adds a check of whether failure-discovery findings depend on the evaluator, while Figure 6 extends the existing perturbation-robustness analysis to another backbone. The training alternatives, attribute breakdowns, reward-attribution analyses, and textual case studies in the appendices remain unchanged.

E5.justification: There are no added or revised repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, significance tests, or uncertainty-estimation procedures. The additional judge and backbone results do not introduce a new statistical reporting practice.

E6.justification: v2 adds GPT-4 evaluation outcomes, RRM robustness scores, and Qwen 2.5 14B results, substantially expanding the evidence for the central empirical findings. New Table 1 reports data-efficiency comparisons, including 46,790 training pairs for REFORM versus 340,296 for RRM on HH. Matched original Mistral results, unperturbed win rates, downstream results, and appendix results are retained.

T1.justification: The failure-mode definition, decoding objectives, metric equations, and Appendix B regularization objective retain their mathematical content. Differences in spacing and bracket rendering do not change the reasoning; no new proofs or formal results appear.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same claims: preference-distribution-agnostic failure discovery, robustness through targeted augmentation, and preservation of reward utility and downstream alignment. The additional experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: Section 5.2 newly interprets the RRM comparison as demonstrating better out-of-distribution robustness with less augmentation data. Existing explanations concerning spurious correlations and the limitations on interpretability and universal robustness remain unchanged.

D1.justification: New Table 1 discloses explicit training-data totals for original reward modeling, REFORM, and RRM; the code link, prompts, and implementation appendix are retained. Its PKU total of 73,907 conflicts with the unchanged 75,077 in Section 4.1, leaving the actual training count unresolved. Detailed recipes for the new Qwen and RRM experiments are not supplied.

R1.justification: The bibliography and related-work sections are retained. RRM, already cited as Liu et al. (2025) in v1, gains a stronger comparative role through the new robustness and data-efficiency positioning in Section 5.2.

P1.justification: The revision adds short passages about dual-judge evaluation and the RRM comparison, with limited caption and terminology edits. The narrative, section sequence, and nearly all existing prose, including the appendices, are retained.

P2.justification: Figures 5 and 6 each expand from two to four panels; Figure 6 also adds RRM bars and revises axes and legends. A new data-efficiency table shifts subsequent table numbers and causes local page reflow. Other figures and appendix displays are retained.

improvement.justification: The second judge, additional backbone, and direct RRM comparison strengthen evidence against evaluator dependence, backbone dependence, and superiority only to an unaugmented control. These are useful gains over v1, but sparse documentation of the new experiments and the conflicting PKU counts in Table 1 and Section 4.1 limit their evidential value. The net improvement is meaningful but limited.
